His eyes narrowing, "Yes," I thought, he'd be around for it, though! I hardly thought he'd come so soon. Who does it happen to be, Lester?"

"Why!" I said, a little impatiently, "it belongs to Armand & Son."

"You've seen their representative," I queried, with a little flush of excitement.

"He came to see me yesterday. I'd like you to meet him, Godfrey. He's Felix Armand, the son of the firm, and one of the most finished gentlemen ever met."

"I'd like to meet him," said Godfrey, smiling queerly. "Perhaps I shall, some day. I hope so, anyway. But how did he explain the blunder, Lester?"

"In some way they shipped the wrong cabinet—Vantine. The right one will get here on Provence to-morrow."

"It is almost interesting," Godfrey commented.

Godfrey added, "I felt yesterday when I was talking with him that perhaps he knew more about this affair than he would admit. I could see that he guessed in an instant who the owner of the letters was, and what they contained. Do you think I ought to hold on to the cabinet a while longer? I could invent some pretext for delay, easily enough."

"Why, no, let him have his cabinet," said Godfrey, with an alacrity that surprised me. "If your theory about it has been exploded, what's the use of hanging on to it?"

"I don't see any use in doing so," I admitted, "but I thought perhaps you might want more time to examine it."

"I've examined it and I'm going to—" Godfrey answered, and I told myself that this was the first time I had ever known him to admit himself wrong. "I'm going," he added, as we parted at the corner.

But I did not see him on the morrow. I was rather expecting a call from him during the morning, and when none came I was certain I should find him awaiting me when I arrived at the Vantine house, in company with Parks. But he was not there, and when I asked for him Parks told me that he had not seen him since the day before.

The old fashioned firemen's tournament was made up of races and other tests of skill between volunteer fire men—dry goods clerks, bookkeepers, plumbers, lawyers, doctors, merchants and bankers who ran with the machine and never got a cent for it. Rivalry was keen between Liberty Hose Company No. 1 on the bottom and Neptune Hose Company No. 1 on the hill. Every small boy in town fairly worshiped the one who set the pace for his teammates as the best sprinter in the vicinity, and there was no less enthusiasm over the lighting couplers. A men's tournament was a notable event for townspeople as well as the "red shirted brave fire ladies" as the Weekly Bazoo always spoke of them.

Then came the paid departments with their horse drawn carts. Originally they were looked upon with much awe, especially in the smaller towns, which, however, showed no less loyalty to their own volunteer companies. As the horse drawn carts became an established feature of the firefighting business in the cities the necessity of recognizing them in firemen's tournaments became evident, so programs were made to include paid department events in addition to the old fashioned competitions among the volunteers. It was in 1902 at Davenport that the horse drawn carts began to take part in state tournaments in Iowa. That was the year that Corbett and Sullivan won the championship for Sioux City. From the start these races were a big feature, and the thrill got more and more pronounced as new complications were added to the contests. The first races were run with the horses harassed at the start. Then came the bunk hitch which involved the spectacular leap from the bed, the slide down the pole, the simultaneous dash of the horses from their stalls to the wagon, the lightning hitch and the getaway amid the cheers of excited thousands. It is doubtful if any other kind of horse race can do as thorough a job of stirring the red blood as a race between the favorite teams of rival cities. It would take a Lew Wallace to begin to do justice to some of those which were run in the halcyon days of Iowa towns. Many have been the sessions in fire houses and elsewhere over the merits of Paddy and Prince and Dick and Charlie and Jack and Mack and Black and Tan, and many have been the wagers that were laid on favorite horses.

Now comes the automobile to rob the great American public of one of the finest thrills it ever has enjoyed. The "motorization" of city fire departments has driven the Corbetts and the Sullivans and the Blacks and the Tans back to the farm and the "bunk hitch" with all its attendant excitement bids fair soon to be a thing of the past. The Iowa state firemen's tournament this year will be held at Maquoketa. Neither Des Moines nor Sioux City will take part. Probably other cities will follow their example.

Most municipalities are gradually replacing their horse drawn trucks with automobile engines and carts. Take away the horses, and you take away the thrill of a race between trucks. Who could imagine community getting as excited over the finest automobile truck ever made as Sioux City and vicinity used to enthuse over good old Corbett and Sullivan?

A wonderful piece of machinery that prints, performs, counts and coils postage stamps, eliminating 10 or 20 processes now necessary, has been exhibited to Administration Officials and members of Congress with a view to their formal approval and assistance in procuring its adoption for the Bureau of Printing and Engraving.

lected.

The regular July meeting of the board of aldermen was held in their rooms in the town building Monday evening at 8 o'clock, with everyone in attendance except Alderman Collins, who is with Co. I. at Mantle. The minutes of the June meeting were taken.

The report of Chief E. H. Richmond of the police department showed 52 arrests during the month of June, as follows: Intoxication 15, assault 6, breach of the peace 1, resistance to officer 2, sale of tobacco to minor 1, intoxication and breach of peace 1, peddling without a license 1, fugitive from justice 1, common drunkard 1, insane 1, vagrancy 2, mittimus 1, suspicious person 4, trespass on railroad 8. 12 were committed to jail, 15 released by the chief, 15 paid fines and costs, judgment suspended 1, otherwise disposed of. 2 lost children were turned over to their parents. 12 tramps were lodged at the station house. The report of E. O. Sumner, superintendent of street, showed that his department expended $1,564.55 from June to July 11 inclusive. The report was accepted. A communication was read from Chief Richmond requesting repairs to the plastering in the police station and extra piping for additional heat in the patrolmen's room. It transpired in the discussion that the plastering was ordered taken down by the first selectman, as it was in a dangerous condition. Later in the meeting a resolution was carried giving the police committee power to make all such necessary changes.

Sidewalk Petitions. Petitions for sidewalks were received from Harry Chasen, Center street; Joseph Delude, Valley and High streets; A. C. Blanchette, Valley street; James H. Hurley, North and Summit street; Frank Bugdee, Bellevue street. The usual course was followed.

The second reading on the following was had: Vanderman Manufacturing Co., Swedish Lutheran church, Laura H. Adams, A. C. Adams, and they were granted.

George and Mary Patton were given leave to withdraw their petition for sidewalk construction.

Hollis H. Lyman was granted a drain-layers license, with the usual requirement as to bond. The application of Charles B. Jordan took the same course.

A petition for the extension of Lebanon avenue some 500 feet was left to the street committee for investigation and report.

A report from the city health officer in regard to an outside vault at the premises, 256 Summit street, and recommending that it be ordered connected with the sewer, was accepted and a resolution passed ordering the same done before September 1, 1914.

Asks Damages for Broken Wrist.

Mayor Dunn read letter from Mrs. Emma Donovan, saying she had a fall April 22 on the corner of Jackson street and broke her left wrist and asking for damages from the city. This matter was referred to committee to investigate and report.

The fire committee was authorized to repair the furnace or purchase a new one for the Bank street engine house, and to repair the roof of the Montgomery Hose company's house.

The public library was ordered closed during the remaining Thursday afternoons and evenings during July and August.

Permission was granted the American Thread company to extend their sewer to discharge their waste into No. 1 pond at their own expense.

The purchasing committee was authorized to purchase 25 carloads of trap rock for use on the city streets.

A resolution was passed to the effect that Chapman street, between Dunham and Ash streets, be repaired and the south retaining wall be rebuilt during the present fiscal year and the street committee was empowered to have the work performed.

A set of rules for the use of the plumbing inspector was presented in a resolution introduced by Alderman Jenkins, and referred to the sanitary committee to investigate and report at the next regular meeting.

Lines and grades of North street from Ash street to Lewiston Avenue were presented to the meeting by the street committee and the same were accepted as read. The street committee's report as to lines and grades on Godfrey street (northerly extension) was accepted as works at Nakohaus School.
